Product Management Career Change Learning Technology Personal Development Week 1: Starting My Product Management Journey as a Final-Year Engineering Student Siddhi Jadhav 4 min read · Oct 17, 2026 -- 1 Listen Share I’m a final-year engineering student aspiring to become a Product Manager. I don’t have an MBA or prior experience in product management, but I’m ready to learn, experiment, and figure things out along the way. And I thought, why not document the journey? If you’re also exploring Product Management, trying to break into the field, or simply curious about what PMs do, welcome! I’m learning too, so consider this a space where we can learn together. I’m Siddhi, and this is Week 1 of my Product Management journey. First Things First: What Is Product Management? You’ve probably used products like WhatsApp, Instagram, or Meesho today. But have you ever wondered who decides which features these apps should have, what problems they should solve, or what improvements should be made next? That’s where Product Management comes in. Product Management sits at the intersection of business, technology, and user needs . A Product Manager helps a team identify the right problems to solve, decide what to build, prioritize improvements, and measure whether the product is creating value for its users and the business. In simple terms, it’s not just about building a product. It’s about building the right product. Why Do We Need Product Managers? Imagine you’re the CEO of a tech company. Your team comes up with an exciting new product idea. The technology is impressive, the team is enthusiastic, and after six months of hard work, the product finally launches. But there’s one problem: nobody wants to use it. Why? Perhaps it doesn’t solve a meaningful problem. Maybe the target users don’t need it, or perhaps the team hasn’t understood what those users actually want. Building something impressive doesn’t automatically make it useful. This is one of the reasons Product Managers matter. They help teams understand users, evaluate opportunities, align product decisions with business goals, and work with different teams to deliver solutions that create value. Of course, even a well-researched product can fail. But understanding the problem before building the solution gives a team a much stronger starting point. How Can I Become a Product Manager Without Prior Experience? This is the question I’m trying to answer myself. As someone entering the field without previous PM experience, I need ways to demonstrate that I can think through product problems, understand users, make decisions, and communicate my reasoning. One approach I’ve been learning about is proof of work . What Is Proof of Work? Think of proof of work as evidence of your abilities. Instead of simply writing “I’m interested in Product Management” on your resume, you can demonstrate that interest through actual work. This could include product teardowns, case studies, user research, product improvement proposals, or a side project that you’ve taken from an initial problem to a tested solution. These projects don’t guarantee an interview, but they can give recruiters and hiring managers something concrete to evaluate. I came across a video explaining how aspiring PMs can build proof of work and create a portfolio. It helped me understand how I could start building mine. My Plan: Three Projects to Get Started After exploring the idea of proof of work, I’ve decided to start with three projects. 1. WhatsApp Product Teardown I use WhatsApp regularly, so I wanted to explore it beyond my everyday user experience. I’ll analyse one of its features, understand the user journey, identify potential friction points, and explore opportunities for improvement. 2. A Product Improvement Proposal for Meesho Recently, I was searching for a yellow dress on Meesho, and finding the specific style I wanted wasn’t as easy as I’d hoped. That experience got me thinking: could a better product tagging and search experience help users find relevant products more easily? I want to explore this problem, understand how users search for products, and evaluate whether my proposed solution would actually help. 3. My First Side Project I also have an idea for a flower-care product that I’m beginning to explore. Rather than immediately jumping into building it, I want to understand the problem, talk to potential users, validate my assumptions, and figure out what a useful first version might look like. I found another video that helped me think about how to approach a PM side project. I’m hoping these projects will help me practise different aspects of Product Management, from analysing existing products to researching user problems and making product decisions. What’s Next? That’s where I am at the end of Week 1. I know I have a lot to learn, and I don’t expect to have everything figured out immediately. For now, my goal is to keep learning, put my knowledge into practice, and document what works, what doesn’t, and what I discover along the way. If you’re also starting your PM journey, I’d love for you to follow along. And if you’ve already been through this process, I’d love to learn from your experiences, too. Next week, I’ll share more about my progress on these projects.
